task_4.title: Fix misleading assertion error when __iter__ raises non-TypeError exceptions
task_4.description: When an object's __iter__ method raises an exception other than TypeError (e.g., ValueError), pytest's assertion rewrite mechanism previously failed to handle it gracefully. This caused the exception to propagate and produce a confusing error message suggesting a faulty __repr__, even though __repr__ was not the issue. The fix broadens the exception handling in the isiterable helper so that any exception raised by iter() causes the object to be treated as non-iterable, preventing the misleading diagnostic message.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when an object's __iter__ method raises any exception (not just TypeError), the assertion introspection mechanism treats the object as non-iterable rather than letting the exception propagate and producing a misleading error message about a faulty __repr__.

expectation.grounded: The isiterable() utility function in the assertion util module must catch Exception (not only TypeError) when calling iter(obj). When any exception is raised by __iter__, isiterable() must return False. During assertion failure reporting, objects whose __iter__ raises non-TypeError exceptions must no longer trigger the 'Probably an object has a faulty __repr__' diagnostic. Instead, the assertion output should display the standard object representation without the erroneous warning.
expectation.conceptual: When an assertion fails involving objects that have a broken or exception-raising __iter__ method, pytest should gracefully fall back to treating those objects as non-iterable. The assertion failure output should show a clean comparison without misleading diagnostic messages about __repr__ being faulty.

constraints.grounded: Objects whose __iter__ raises TypeError must continue to be treated as non-iterable (existing behavior preserved). Objects that are genuinely iterable (whose iter() call succeeds) must still be recognized as iterable. Text objects (str) must still be excluded from iterable treatment by the istext() check. The broader exception handling must not suppress exceptions outside the isiterable check — only exceptions raised during the iter() probe within isiterable() are affected.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must not alter the behavior for objects that are legitimately iterable or for objects that were already correctly identified as non-iterable. Only the error-handling path for unexpected exceptions during the iterability check is affected. No other assertion rewriting or reporting behavior should change.

behavior: When iter(obj) raises TypeError inside isiterable(), the function returns False (unchanged behavior).
When iter(obj) raises any other exception (e.g., ValueError, RuntimeError) inside isiterable(), the function now returns False instead of letting the exception propagate.

Assertion failure messages for objects with exception-raising __iter__ methods no longer include the misleading 'representation of details failed' / 'Probably an object has a faulty __repr__' diagnostic.
Assertion failure output for such objects displays the standard object repr comparison cleanly.
acceptance_criteria: Given a class whose __iter__ raises ValueError, when an assertion comparing two instances of that class fails, then the failure message should show the standard repr comparison without any 'faulty __repr__' warning.
Given a class whose __iter__ raises RuntimeError, when an assertion involving that class fails, then no unhandled exception from __iter__ should appear in the output.
Given a class whose __iter__ raises TypeError, when an assertion involving that class fails, then the object is treated as non-iterable (existing behavior unchanged).
Given a normally iterable object (e.g., a list), when an assertion comparison fails, then the detailed iterable diff is still produced as before.
When isiterable() is called on a string, it still returns False regardless of the exception handling change.

task_1.title: Fix non-string constants mistakenly detected as docstrings during assertion rewriting
task_1.description: On Python >= 3.8, the AST represents all constants (strings, integers, floats, etc.) using the same node type (ast.Constant). The assertion rewriter's docstring detection logic did not verify that the constant value was actually a string before treating it as a docstring. When a test file began with a non-string constant (e.g., an integer literal), the rewriter would pass that value to a string-containment check ('PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE' in docstring), raising a TypeError and preventing test collection. The fix adds a type check on the extracted constant value to ensure only actual string constants are treated as docstrings.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that test files beginning with non-string constant expressions (e.g., integer or float literals as the first statement) are collected and executed correctly without raising a TypeError during assertion rewriting on Python >= 3.8.

expectation.grounded: When the AssertionRewriter processes a module whose first expression is a non-string ast.Constant (e.g., an integer), the rewriter must skip that expression rather than treating it as a docstring. The is_rewrite_disabled check must only be called with a str value. The _get_ast_constant_value helper must return the underlying value of an AST constant node, and the caller must verify the value is a str before proceeding with docstring logic.
expectation.conceptual: When a test file starts with a non-string constant expression (such as a bare integer, float, or other non-string literal), pytest's assertion rewriting should silently ignore that expression and continue processing the file normally, without raising any errors during test collection.

constraints.grounded: Files that start with a valid string docstring containing 'PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE' must still correctly disable assertion rewriting. The fix must handle both Python >= 3.8 (ast.Constant) and older Python versions (ast.Str) without regression. The is_rewrite_disabled method must never receive a non-string argument.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must not break existing docstring-based assertion rewrite suppression. Test files that legitimately use string docstrings (including the PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE directive) must continue to behave as before. The solution must work across all supported Python versions.

behavior: When a Python file's first expression is a non-string constant (int, float, bytes, etc.), the assertion rewriter no longer treats it as a docstring and does not raise a TypeError.
When a Python file's first expression is a string constant, it is still correctly recognized as a docstring and checked for the PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE directive.
The constant value extraction from AST nodes is version-aware, using the appropriate attribute for Python >= 3.8 versus older versions.
Test collection succeeds for files that begin with numeric or other non-string constant expressions on Python >= 3.8.
acceptance_criteria: When a test file starts with a bare integer literal (e.g., 1) as its first statement, pytest collects and runs the file without raising TypeError during assertion rewriting.
When a test file starts with a bare float literal as its first statement, pytest collects and runs the file without error.
When a test file starts with a string docstring containing 'PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE', assertion rewriting is correctly disabled for that file.
When a test file starts with a normal string docstring (without 'PYTEST_DONT_REWRITE'), assertion rewriting proceeds normally and the docstring is recognized.
When running on Python >= 3.8, all of the above behaviors hold correctly given that constants are represented as ast.Constant nodes.
When using 'pytest -k <pattern>' to filter tests, files beginning with non-string constants do not cause collection errors.

task_5.title: Standardize documentation to use hyphenated CLI option names
task_5.description: Documentation and internal docstrings inconsistently referred to CLI options using their non-hyphenated aliases (--junitxml, --collectonly) instead of the canonical hyphenated forms (--junit-xml, --collect-only). This caused user confusion because --help and the reference docs showed the hyphenated form while examples and docstrings used the non-hyphenated alias. All documentation references were updated to consistently use the hyphenated option names.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that all documentation, docstrings, and code examples consistently refer to CLI options using their canonical hyphenated forms (--junit-xml instead of --junitxml, --collect-only instead of --collectonly) to eliminate confusion about whether these are separate options or aliases.

expectation.grounded: The docstring of the Pytester.inline_genitems method should reference --collect-only (not --collectonly). The docstring of the no-op record_func inside record_testsuite_property should reference --junit-xml (not --junitxml). All user-facing documentation strings for CLI options should use the hyphenated canonical form that matches the output of pytest --help.
expectation.conceptual: All documentation surfaces — including API docstrings, user guides, and inline code examples — should present CLI options in their canonical hyphenated form. Users reading any documentation should see a single consistent spelling for each option, matching what pytest --help displays.

constraints.grounded: Both hyphenated and non-hyphenated forms of the CLI options (--junit-xml / --junitxml, --collect-only / --collectonly) must remain valid at runtime as aliases. No CLI argument parsing logic or runtime behavior should be modified. Only documentation and docstring text should change.
constraints.conceptual: This change must be purely cosmetic and documentary. No existing CLI invocations should break, and both alias forms must continue to be accepted. The functional behavior of all affected fixtures and test utilities must remain identical.

behavior: The Pytester.inline_genitems docstring now shows --collect-only instead of --collectonly when describing the command it runs internally.
The record_testsuite_property fixture's internal no-op function docstring now references --junit-xml instead of --junitxml.
No runtime behavior, argument parsing, or test output changes occur — both alias forms continue to work identically.
acceptance_criteria: When inspecting the docstring of Pytester.inline_genitems, it should contain '--collect-only' and not '--collectonly'.
When inspecting the docstring of the no-op record_func inside record_testsuite_property, it should contain '--junit-xml' and not '--junitxml'.
When running pytest --collect-only or pytest --collectonly, both forms should still be accepted and produce identical behavior.
When running pytest --junit-xml=path or pytest --junitxml=path, both forms should still be accepted and produce identical output.
No functional test regressions should occur as a result of these documentation-only changes.

task_3.title: Fix collection error tracebacks not being pruned
task_3.description: A regression in pytest 7.4 caused tracebacks from collection errors to not be pruned. When a test module raises an exception during collection, the traceback should be cut down to show only user-relevant frames. Instead, the full internal pytest traceback was displayed, including frames from internal modules like runner, python, pathlib, assertion rewrite, and importlib bootstrap. The fix ensures the pruned traceback is used when filtering, rather than the original unpruned traceback.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that when a test module raises an exception during collection, the resulting traceback is pruned to exclude pytest-internal frames. Prior to this fix, a regression caused the Collector to discard its own traceback pruning, resulting in verbose tracebacks that exposed internal call chains (runner, import machinery, assertion rewrite) instead of showing only the user-relevant frames at the point of failure.

expectation.grounded: When the Collector._repr_failure_ method processes a collection error, the traceback returned by its pruning logic (via Traceback.cut on path and excludepath, followed by Traceback.filter) must apply the filter on the already-cut ntraceback, not on the original excinfo.traceback. The resulting ExceptionInfo representation should contain only frames from the user's test module and the immediate raise site, excluding frames from internal pytest modules.
expectation.conceptual: When a test module fails during collection (e.g., raises an exception at module level), the error output should show a short, pruned traceback containing only the user's code and the exception, not a long traceback full of pytest internal frames. The traceback pruning that was already implemented must actually take effect rather than being silently discarded.

constraints.grounded: The fix must not alter the behavior when traceback cutting produces no change (the fallback to excludepath-based cutting and the final fallback returning excinfo.traceback must remain intact). The Traceback.cut and Traceback.filter APIs must continue to be used in sequence. No change to the public ExceptionInfo or Traceback interfaces is required.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must only correct the traceback pruning for collection errors. It must not affect traceback display for test execution failures, nor change the fallback behavior when pruning is not applicable. Existing traceback cutting and filtering logic must be preserved.

behavior: When a test module raises an exception at import time during collection, the displayed traceback is pruned to show only the user's module frame and the exception, excluding all internal pytest frames.
The Collector's traceback pruning pipeline (cut then filter) now correctly chains operations on the pruned traceback rather than discarding the pruned result.
The fallback path where traceback cutting has no effect (ntraceback == traceback) still applies excludepath-based cutting before filtering.
When no cutting is applicable, the original excinfo.traceback is returned unmodified, preserving existing fallback behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a test module contains a top-level 'raise Exception(...)' and is collected by pytest, the ERROR traceback output should contain only the user's module frame and the exception line, with no internal pytest frames visible.

When a collection error occurs, the traceback should not contain frames from internal modules such as runner, python collector internals, pathlib import utilities, importlib bootstrap, or assertion rewrite.
When traceback pruning by path has no effect, the fallback excludepath-based pruning should still be applied before filtering.
Normal test execution failures (not collection errors) should continue to display tracebacks as before, unaffected by this change.

task_2.title: Fix ValueError when faulthandler teardown encounters closed stderr
task_2.description: During pytest shutdown, the faulthandler plugin attempted to re-enable faulthandler by querying sys.stderr or sys.__stderr__ for a file descriptor. In certain environments or plugin configurations, these streams could already be closed at teardown time, causing a ValueError ('I/O operation on closed file'). The fix captures the stderr file descriptor early during pytest_configure, while the streams are still valid, and reuses that stashed descriptor during pytest_unconfigure instead of querying the potentially-closed streams at teardown.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the faulthandler plugin does not raise a ValueError during pytest teardown when sys.stderr and sys.__stderr__ have already been closed. Previously, calling get_stderr_fileno() at unconfigure time would fail if another plugin or the runtime had already closed the standard error streams, resulting in an unhandled ValueError that surfaced to the user as a crash at the end of a test session.

expectation.grounded: During pytest_configure, the faulthandler plugin should capture the stderr file descriptor number via get_stderr_fileno() and stash it using the fault_handler_original_stderr_fd_key StashKey (only when faulthandler.is_enabled() is True at startup). During pytest_unconfigure, when re-enabling faulthandler for sessions where it was originally enabled, the plugin should use the stashed file descriptor integer directly via faulthandler.enable() rather than calling get_stderr_fileno(). The fault_handler_originally_enabled_key StashKey[bool] should be replaced by fault_handler_original_stderr_fd_key StashKey[int], combining the 'was enabled' flag and the original fd into one entry whose presence indicates original enablement.
expectation.conceptual: The faulthandler plugin should snapshot the stderr file descriptor at session startup while standard error is known to be open. At teardown, it should restore faulthandler to the original descriptor without re-querying the standard error streams, which may no longer be available. This ensures graceful shutdown regardless of whether other components have closed stderr before pytest finishes its unconfigure sequence.

constraints.grounded: The get_stderr_fileno() function must not be called during pytest_unconfigure. The stashed file descriptor in fault_handler_original_stderr_fd_key must only be set when faulthandler.is_enabled() returns True at configure time. The duplicated fd stored in fault_handler_stderr_fd_key must still be properly closed via os.close() during unconfigure. Both stash entries must be deleted from config.stash after use to avoid resource leaks. The faulthandler.enable() call at unconfigure must receive the stashed integer fd directly, not a file object.
constraints.conceptual: Teardown must not depend on the runtime state of standard error streams. Resource cleanup of duplicated file descriptors must still occur. The fix must not alter the faulthandler behavior during the actual test session — only the configure and unconfigure lifecycle is affected. Sessions where faulthandler was not originally enabled must not attempt to re-enable it at teardown.

behavior: At pytest_configure, the stderr file descriptor is captured once via get_stderr_fileno() and stashed for later use, rather than being re-derived at teardown.

The presence of fault_handler_original_stderr_fd_key in config.stash implicitly indicates that faulthandler was originally enabled, replacing the previous boolean flag fault_handler_originally_enabled_key.
At pytest_unconfigure, faulthandler.enable() is called with the stashed integer file descriptor instead of calling get_stderr_fileno(), avoiding any access to sys.stderr or sys.__stderr__.
When faulthandler was not originally enabled, no re-enable call is made at teardown (fault_handler_original_stderr_fd_key is absent from the stash).
The duplicated file descriptor (fault_handler_stderr_fd_key) is still closed and removed from the stash during unconfigure, preserving existing cleanup behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When sys.stderr and sys.__stderr__ are both closed before pytest_unconfigure runs, the teardown completes without raising a ValueError.
When faulthandler was originally enabled at session start and stderr streams are closed at teardown, faulthandler is still successfully re-enabled using the stashed file descriptor.
When faulthandler was not originally enabled at session start, no attempt is made to re-enable it during teardown regardless of stderr stream state.

When stderr streams remain open throughout the session, the faulthandler configure/unconfigure lifecycle behaves identically to before the fix — faulthandler is enabled during the session and restored afterward.
The duplicated file descriptor created via os.dup() is properly closed during pytest_unconfigure, with no file descriptor leaks.
Given a plugin or fixture that closes sys.stderr during the test session, when pytest reaches unconfigure, then it should complete without error and exit cleanly.
